summary: DCD now makes up most UK deceased donation (792 of 1,428 deceased donors in 2025/26, NHSBT), while consent/authorisation fell to 57% overall and about 53% for DCD. Law: Wales (own Act, deemed consent from 1 Dec 2015), England (Organ Donation (Deemed Consent) Act 2019 amending HTA 2004 s3(6)(ba)/(6A)/(6B), from 20 May 2020), Scotland (Human Tissue (Authorisation) (Scotland) Act 2019, deemed authorisation from 26 Mar 2021) and Northern Ireland (2022 Act inserting HTA s3(6AA)/(9A); deemed consent in effect from 1 June 2023). In England consent is deemed unless a person in a qualifying relationship provides information that would lead a reasonable person to conclude the person would not have consented; HTA Code F says relatives have no legal right to revoke a valid decision but donation need not proceed where public confidence is at risk. Excepted adults include those who lacked capacity to understand deemed consent for a significant period before death (HTA guidance: 12 months), which captures many PDOC patients. Pre-mortem steps in England/Wales rest on MCA best interests per DH 2009 guidance (heparin, resuscitation, femoral cannulation unlikely ever to be in best interests; seek Court of Protection declaration); the 2021 UK NRP protocol says no pre-mortem interventions are currently allowed in controlled DCD. Scotland alone has a statutory pre-death procedures regime (Type A: SSI 2020/80; Type B incl. CT, MRI, bronchoscopy, needing two doctors independent of retrieval: SSI 2021/110); heparin is on neither list. The 2025 AoMRC Code leaves the five-minute observation unchanged (circulatory criteria not in its list of major changes) but specifies ventilator disconnection before the five minutes, start at mechanical asystole (arterial line or echo acceptable; ECG asystole not required), corneal reflexes recommended soon after arrest, independence from retrieval, and that post-mortem perfusion protocols must ensure no blood circulation to the brain. Dhanani NEJM 2021 (631 patients) found transient cardiac activity after pulselessness in 14% on waveform review, all within 4 min 20 s; a 2023 systematic review rated five minutes sufficient for controlled DCD (moderate certainty). A-NRP is being rolled out nationally by 2027 with NICE guidance due Nov 2026; TA-NRP remains contested (ACP 2021 call for a pause; UK-Canadian permanence proposal; retrospective data showing less severe PGD). Uncontrolled DCD is a Cambridge pilot only. The RCP 2020 PDOC guideline states donation is not possible after CANH withdrawal. Of 1,037 consented DCD patients in 2025/26, 266 did not donate, 52% of them because of prolonged time to asystole; length of process was the commonest family reason for declining DCD (20%).
takeaways: Make the withdrawal decision first, on its own merits in the patient's best interests, independently of donation, and document it.

Under deemed consent the family's role is to give information about the patient's own view; check excepted-adult status (lack of capacity for a significant period, HTA guidance 12 months), which often applies in PDOC.

Pre-mortem steps must be in the patient's best interests and not cause harm or distress; under the current (2021) national NRP protocol there is no pre-mortem heparin or cannulation in UK controlled DCD, and Scotland has a statutory Type A/Type B list.
Confirm death after five full minutes, off the ventilator, observed in person, by a clinician independent of the retrieval team, as the 2025 AoMRC Code sets out.
Families most often decline DCD because the process takes too long; plan logistics early and be honest about timescales.
